claims.claim: 1-year primary unassisted patency 49% ePTFE AVG, 62% AVF
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Only found as an unreferenced sentence in a patent (US 9,023,377): "the 1-year primary unassisted access patency rates were 49% for vascular access structures such as arteriovenous grafts involving ePTFE prosthetic bridges and 62% for arteriovenous (AV) fistulae", listed next to a bare 'US Renal Data System' bullet (opened via Google Patents; no author, journal, year). No peer-reviewed study or USRDS table with that pair found. Contrary figures: USRDS ADR 2021 ch.4 (via search snippet only, page not opened): cumulative incidence of loss of primary unassisted patency at 1 y 51.8% for AVF (2016-18 starters) and 69.2% for AVG, i.e. about 48% / 31% patent. KDOQI 2019 (opened): loss of primary unassisted patency for grafts 'as high as 75% by 1 year' (from a review text). Do not cite 49/62 as a study result.
claims.note: Population/definition unknown. Also snippet-only: JVS 2018 (Al-Jaishi) unadjusted 1-y primary patency 43.3% AVF vs 31.5% AVG.

claims.claim: 30% to 70% of AV fistulae suffer primary failure
claims.correct_value_or_quote: KDOQI 2019 Vascular Access guideline (PDF opened, text extracted): "20% to 60% of AVFs created fail to mature successfully for dialysis use." Also: "AVF maturation failure ... has been reported in observational studies to range from 20% to 60%" and a US multicentre RCT reported "up to 60%". Guideline also notes primary failure is 'inconsistently defined'. Snippet-only: a meta-analysis pooled 23% (95% CI 18-28%); some papers quote 9-70%.
claims.note: Use '20-60% (observational), pooled ~23% in a meta-analysis' not 30-70%.

claims.claim: FFS Medicare paid ~$2.8B for dialysis vascular access services in 2013, ~12% of ESRD payments
claims.correct_value_or_quote: "Overall, in 2013, fee-for-service Medicare paid $2.8 billion for dialysis vascular access-related services, ~12% of all end-stage renal disease payments." Abstract retrieved via Europe PMC API (PubMed page itself blocked by cookie wall). Setting: elderly US Medicare patients initiating HD 2010-2011; also 'only 54% of AVFs were successfully used for HD' and cost 2-4x higher after patency loss/non-use.
claims.note: Paper: Medicare Costs Associated With AVFs Among US Hemodialysis Patients, AJKD 2018. 2013 figure is a paper estimate, not a USRDS table; it is 13 years old.

claims.claim: Total Medicare dialysis spending $48.9B in 2022, ~7% of Medicare budget for <1% of beneficiaries
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Could not find $48.9B anywhere. USRDS 2025 ADR (search snippet only; ADR page is JavaScript-rendered and I could not open its text): "Total Medicare costs for ESRD: $55.3 billion in 2023 (ESRD Volume, Figure 9.2a)"; 45% of new ESRD patients had FFS in 2023 (55% Medicare Advantage); 54% of all ESRD patients FFS; MA claims only through 2022. MedPAC (snippet only): FFS Medicare spending for dialysis, dialysis drugs and ESRD labs $8.8B in 2022; FFS ESRD expenditures fell 8% 2022 to 2023 as MA enrolment grew. CRS (snippet only): ESRD ~7% of Medicare FFS spending vs ~1% of enrolment (FFS+MA). Newer year exists: 2025 ADR (released Dec 2025) covers 2023 data; a 2026 ADR partial release (15 Oct 2026, opened) includes ESRD ch.9 but I could not read its figures.
claims.note: The 7%/1% is ESRD (not dialysis only) and FFS-based. Pull the number from ADR Vol 2 ch.9 in a browser before pitching; scope (ESRD vs dialysis, FFS vs all) of $48.9B unresolved.

claims.claim: Haemodialysis is done three to five times a week
claims.correct_value_or_quote: KDOQI 2019 vascular access guideline (opened): "the typical thrice-weekly dialysis sessions" and "a conventional dialysis prescription of three times a week dialysis, for 3-4 hours per treatment"; it notes newer definitions also apply to incremental, short daily and nocturnal HD. Say 'typically three times a week in-centre; more frequent regimens exist (short daily, nocturnal, home)'. 'Three to five' is not the in-centre norm. I did not open the KDOQI 2015 HD adequacy guideline.

claims.claim: AV grafts fail predominantly by stenosis at venous anastomosis from neointimal hyperplasia
claims.correct_value_or_quote: KDOQI 2019 (opened): "Thrombosis accounts for almost 80% of AVG failures due to an underlying stenosis at the venous anastomosis." PMC8108319 review (opened, first 100k chars): "venous neointimal hyperplasia at the venous anastomotic site" named as the predominant cause of graft failure (ref 44).
claims.note: Second source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8108319/

claims.claim: Low/oscillatory WSS at anastomosis associated with IH, documented on histology at AVG venous anastomosis; contrary evidence
claims.correct_value_or_quote: No primary paper opened that links measured low/oscillatory WSS to histology at human AVG venous anastomoses. All below from search snippets, pages not opened: baboon study of tissue-engineered vs PTFE AV grafts says IH 'has also been identified in regions with turbulent flow, flow separation, low shear stress, and oscillatory shear' (hemodynamics cited from prior work); a patient-CT CFD study says oscillatory WSS 'is believed to be the main' trigger (computational, no histology); a bypass-graft multiscale model found low TAWSS (<0.5 Pa) 'did not always correspond to regions of NIH progression'. CONTRARY (snippets): a review notes 'regions with high wall shear stresses (5-10 Pa) correspond to NIH formation'; porcine shunt study tied high WSS and gradients to hyperplasia and wall stiffening (preliminary histology); one cited study found an 'inverse correlation between WSS (5-80 Pa peak) and stenosis'; the review calls shear's mechanistic role 'unclear'. Other proposed drivers: vessel injury, PTFE compliance mismatch, graft bioincompatibility, uremia. PMC8108319 (opened) only says WSS affects AVF remodelling and may contribute to juxta-anastomotic stenosis.
claims.note: Pitch should say 'hypothesised and partly supported; evidence mixed, includes high-shear findings', not established. Candidate sources to open next: PMC3175038, PMC4189833, doi 10.1038/s42003-021-02065-6.

extra_findings: Companies and products (all snippet-level, no manufacturer page opened): Gore (ePTFE grafts; Acuseal and Propaten named in a Chinese retrospective comparing Propaten, Acuseal and Venaflo II: no significant difference in primary, assisted primary or secondary patency); Bard/BD (Venaflo, cuffed). I found nothing on Getinge/Maquet, LeMaitre (Artegraft), Terumo or Humacyte HAV for dialysis access; Humacyte Symvess surfaced only for extremity trauma. Not verified.

Cuffed grafts: randomized study of 89 ePTFE grafts, cuffed Venaflo vs non-cuffed Stretch Gore-Tex, 12-month primary patency 56% vs 41%, secondary 91% vs 78% (journal and authors not shown in snippet). Lemson et al, J Vasc Surg 2000 RCT of a venous cuff: fewer thrombotic occlusions but comparable primary and secondary patency; authors advised against routine use. Mansoura RCT NCT03405233 (double-cuffed vs single vs none), status unknown.

Helical/flow-modifying: SwirlGraft (Veryan Medical per Dutch registry; ISRCTN11502523): Huijbregts et al., 20 patients, 6-month primary/assisted/secondary patency 57.9+/-11.4%, 84.4+/-8.3%, 100%; some grafts partly lost helical geometry. Johannesburg 2024 retrospective of the 'Spiral Flow' graft, 80 grafts/71 patients, 1-year primary 54%, secondary 63%. No RCT found. A helical-design CFD paper (Polito) says in-vivo deformation could cancel the benefit. Snippet-level only.

Adjacent venous-anastomosis devices (not geometry grafts): InterGraft connector single-arm study (cumulative patency 92.08% at 6 months, primary unassisted 60.21%); Phraxis EndoForce FDA approved 15 May 2025; Merit WRAPSODY FDA approved 19 Dec 2024 for outflow stenosis incl. AVG venous anastomosis. Snippet-level.

Competitive gap relevant to pitch: I found no trial showing a geometry-modified graft clearly beating standard ePTFE; the one cuffed RCT favourable, one not. Frame the sweep as hypothesis generation, not a clinical claim.

could_not_check: USRDS 2025 and 2026 ADR chapter 9 text (JS-rendered, WebFetch returned only the title); so the exact scope of $48.9B and the 2022/2023 dialysis-only figures are unverified.
The ADR 2021 ch.4 patency numbers (snippet only).
AJKD 2025 Core Curriculum and AJKD 2025 ADR summary (403 / not fetched).
The patent's cited original source for 49%/62%; page text beyond the first 100k characters not read; scanned PDF version has no text layer.

Original histology studies for C7; manufacturer and FDA pages for graft makers; KDOQI 2015 HD adequacy guideline; Huijbregts SwirlGraft paper and the cuffed Venaflo RCT originals (only search snippets seen).

claims.claim: 1997 JVS study: optimised end-to-side anastomosis geometry roughly halves WSS gradients vs standard and Taylor patch
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Lei M, Archie JP, Kleinstreuer C. 'Computational design of a bypass graft that minimizes wall shear stress gradients in the region of the distal anastomosis.' J Vasc Surg 1997;25(4):637-646, PMID 9129618, DOI 10.1016/s0741-5214(97)70289-1. Abstract (PubMed record via Europe PMC): 'The optimized design reduces wall shear stress gradients to almost one half of that of the standard and Taylor patch geometries.' Also: 'At resting flow the Taylor patch produces slightly lower wall shear stress gradients ... than the standard end-to-side anastomosis. At exercise flow wall shear stress gradients almost triple in the standard anastomosis and increase approximately 30% in the Taylor patch.' Method: 'transient three-dimensional ... laminar incompressible blood flow'; optimum 'obtained iteratively by minimizing the local wall shear stress gradients'; 'assuming idealized merging of the graft with the artery'.
claims.note: Verified from the abstract text in the PubMed record (Europe PMC API). Full text not opened. Caveats for the pitch: this is a peripheral arterial bypass (graft-to-artery) distal anastomosis, not an AV graft venous anastomosis; it is a single idealised geometry, a metric (time-averaged WSS gradient, not TAWSS/OSI/RRT), laminar CFD, and the 'almost one half' is the abstract's wording, not a precise percentage. It is also itself an optimisation study (iterative), so it is prior art for shape optimisation of anastomoses.

claims.claim: 2025 CFD study of helical graft designs analysed 27 models across anastomosis angle, helical diameter, helical pitch
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Benitez J, Monzon J, Abenojar WJ, Honra J, Tayo L. 'Computational Fluid Dynamics Analysis of Blood Flow in Helical Arterio-Venous Bypass Graft for Enhanced Flow Performance.' Applied Sciences 2025, 15(20), 11064, published 15 Oct 2025, DOI 10.3390/app152011064. Abstract: '...from twenty-seven graft models changing anastomosis angles, helical diameters, and helical pitches. Model 25-13-30 (25-degree anastomosis angle, 13 mm helical diameter, 30 mm helical pitch) demonstrated the most favorable overall hemodynamic performance'. Levels: angles 25/35/45 deg, 3 helical diameters, 3 pitches (3x3x3). Solver: 'ANSYS Fluent 2025 Student Version'; 'both steady-state and transient CFD simulation'. Stage 1 steady on the models (AWA-WSS, pressure drop, helicity); the 'four (4) best' went to stage 2 transient (TAWSS, OSI, RRT). Laminar model, Carreau non-Newtonian (zero-shear 0.056 Pa s, infinite-shear 0.0035 Pa s), 'vessel walls were modeled as rigid', constant inlet 0.3 m/s for steady, pulsatile profile taken from literature for transient. 'An average number of 430,000 elements' hybrid mesh. Transient: 'executed for three initial periods ... data sampling was performed during the fourth period. Each period consisted of 25 time steps, with a maximum of 20 iterations per time step.' Runtime per case: not stated (searched the full text for time/hours/CPU; no mention).
claims.note: Full-text PDF opened and read via the MDPI file mirror (the article HTML returned 403). Abstract also confirmed from Crossref. Note the paper itself says it validated pressure/velocity against a reference with 0% inlet and 18.69% outlet velocity discrepancy and lists rigid-wall and laminar assumptions as limitations; its own text says earlier helical work 'did not investigate other influential parameters, such as helical pitch'.

claims.claim: Nobody has searched the anastomosis design space exhaustively; published studies compare small numbers of designs (refutation attempt)
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Partly false as phrased. Optimisation/surrogate work on AV access geometry exists, but at ~100-geometry scale, not thousands. (1) AV GRAFT, surrogate global optimisation: Quicken S, Delhaas T, Mees BME, Huberts W. 'Haemodynamic optimisation of a dialysis graft design using a global optimisation approach.' Int J Numer Method Biomed Eng 2021;37(2):e3423, DOI 10.1002/cnm.3423. 'A total of 103 successful simulations were performed' (112 geometries generated, 2 rejected, 6 crashed); meta-models (polynomial chaos) replaced CFD, 'reduced the total number of CFD evaluations ... by roughly a factor of 2000'; optimiser sequential quadratic programming from 1000 random starts; OASIS/FEniCS pulsatile solver, 2.7-4.7 million tetrahedral elements, dt 1e-4 s, 'Average simulation time of each CFD simulation was 77 hours'; helical centreline + helical ridge design. (2) AV FISTULA, Kriging/MADS: Grechy et al. Physics of Fluids 2017;29(10) 'Suppressing unsteady flow in arterio-venous fistulae' uses 'a Mesh Adaptive Direct Search optimisation framework' and 'Results constitute the first use of numerical optimisation to design a device'; the author's PhD thesis (Imperial) describes 'A Kriging-based optimisation methodology' (Latin hypercube sampling used) and, separately, 'Patient specific simulations on 60 reconstructed AVF' (steady). The figure '91 simulations' for the Kriging surrogate appears only in a secondary citation (Sci Rep 2023 NeoVAD paper snippet). (3) AV fistula shape optimisation: Mahmoudzadeh Akherat et al., Comput Methods Appl Mech Eng 2017;321:46-69, BOBYQA gradient-free, 'between 1,000 and 10,000 cost-function evaluations' but steady 2D/3D COMSOL on a handful of patients, not a design-space sweep. (4) Bypass anastomosis GA + meshless CFD (PubMed 20166238) and Lei 1997 (see P1). (5) AV graft angle optimisation: Williams et al. Sci Rep 2021 simulated 6 angles (90, 60, 45, 30, 15, 13 deg) and 'Optimizations predicted that an intermediate ... angle was optimal'. (6) AV graft curvature: arXiv 2508.06148 (Wang, Abadie, Wall, Perez Esteban 2025): 6 straight + 9 looped angle models in OpenFOAM. Review (JASN 2026, PMC13337174) Table 3 lists 17, 4, 3, 2, 16, 36 and 2 models for geometry studies and says 'The page reports no ML surrogate trained on CFD outputs' (my reading of the page; review is secondary).
claims.note: Largest numbers found: AV graft = 103 simulated designs (Quicken 2021, opened in PMC). AV fistula = 60 patient-specific steady cases (Grechy thesis front matter, opened) and 91 (secondary only). Non-AV vascular graft = 2000 high-fidelity models per patient for Fontan graft design (Liu et al., IEEE TBME 2022, PMC8753752: 'to run 2,000 high-fidelity models, which took approximately 15 hours for each patient'; Gaussian process surrogate + pattern search; OpenFOAM simpleFoam steady; 10-D design space; n=2 patients). No source found describing a sweep of thousands of AV-graft venous-anastomosis geometries, nor any GPU/LBM geometry sweep. Safer pitch wording: 'prior optimisation used ~10^2 CFD runs (Quicken 2021: 103 designs, ~77 h per run); we aim for ~10^3-10^4 at far lower cost per run.' Absence claims are limited by what I could search; I could not open the Kriging 91 count, and did not search non-English or patent literature thoroughly.

claims.claim: Any prior work using lattice Boltzmann or GPU for AV graft/fistula (what the project proposes)
claims.correct_value_or_quote: LBM for AV access exists, but not as a geometry sweep and not GPU. (a) McCullough JWS, Coveney PV. 'High fidelity blood flow in a patient-specific arteriovenous fistula', arXiv 2012.04639 (v2 Jun 2021): HemeLB lattice Boltzmann, forearm vasculature; 'discretised to a resolution of dx = 50 um, resulting in a total of 6,128,855 lattice sites in the arterial geometry and 16,767,772 in the venous geometry'; 'time step of dt = 3 us'; 'run for a total of 1.1 million time steps ... 3.3 s of physical time'; 'each took approximately 2 hours of wall time to run on 50 nodes (2400 cores)' on SuperMUC-NG (CPU supercomputer; the arXiv text I read does not mention GPU); 'We assume that solid walls are rigid'; single patient model. (b) Bai Z, Zhu L. Physics of Fluids 2021;33:051905 'Simulation of blood flow past distal arteriovenous-graft anastomosis with intimal hyperplasia': 'Navier-Stokes equations which are numerically solved by the lattice Boltzmann model (D3Q19). The fluid-structure interaction is modeled by the immersed boundary framework', pulsatile. (c) Bai & Zhu, Physics of Fluids 2019;31(9):091902 (AVG graft-vein diameter ratio, attaching angle, Re up to several hundreds, compliant model) and Computers & Fluids 2019;181:403 (compliant AVG anastomosis). These are small parametric studies (a few dimensionless parameters), AVG-specific and LB-IB based.
claims.note: (a) opened as PDF and text-extracted; (b) and (c) abstracts read from Crossref records, full text not opened, so number of cases in the Bai & Zhu studies is unknown. A web-search summary suggested a GPU HemeLB code (CUDA); I did not open any GPU HemeLB paper and the AVF paper itself ran on CPU nodes, so GPU+AVG remains 'not found', not 'proven absent'. So a pitch line 'nobody has used LBM for AV grafts' would be wrong; 'nobody has used GPU LBM to sweep thousands of AVG geometries' is not contradicted by anything I found.

claims.claim: Typical AVG flow rates, diameters, velocities and Reynolds numbers at the venous anastomosis
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Loth F, Fischer PF, Bassiouny HS. 'Blood Flow in End-to-Side Anastomoses.' Annu Rev Fluid Mech 2008;40:367-393 (PMC12577737): 'Flow rates for AV grafts typically range from 1000-2000 ml min-1'; 'AV grafts are synthetic, with typical diameters of 6 mm and lengths of 15-20 cm'; 'Reynolds numbers based on the graft diameter and mean flow in the range Re = 900-1800' (arterial bypass: 'Re = 100-300'). Recent CFD inputs differ: Williams et al. Sci Rep 2021 (PMC8190231): 700 mL/min into graft, artery 4 mm, vein 8 mm, graft tapering 4 to 7 mm, Re about 1800, venous return 15 cm/s centreline; Wang et al. arXiv 2508.06148 (2025): mean 841.5 mL/min, 4 mm artery, arterial inlet 1.12 m/s giving Re = 949.76, venous 0.15 m/s ('strictly under laminar condition'); Quicken 2021: mean 1.06x10^3 mL/min, vein 7.7 mm, artery 6.6 mm, graft 6.0 mm. So 'typical' spans roughly 700-2000 mL/min, Re roughly 900-1800.
claims.note: All values read from opened pages. The 2008 review's 1000-2000 mL/min is higher than the 700-840 mL/min used in the 2021/2025 CFD papers; state a range, not a single number. Dialysis AVG flow-monitoring guideline values (e.g. KDOQI) were not checked.

claims.claim: Evidence that flow at the venous anastomosis is transitional or turbulent
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Sources disagree. For: Loth et al. 2008 review: 'Under certain conditions, the high flow rates can lead to transitional or weakly turbulent flow states' and 'AV graft flows can potentially be turbulent throughout the cardiac cycle'; 'vibrations with frequencies greater than 100 Hz that are attributed to weakly turbulent flow conditions'; Shu & Hwang reported 'a 100-Hz pressure fluctuation and palpable thrill at the venous anastomosis'. Against/mixed: same review: at Re = 1060 'LDA measurements indicated small fluctuations distal to the toe, whereas the numerical results indicated steady flow'; at Re = 1200 pulsatile 'only low-frequency (30-40 Hz) velocity fluctuations that indicated laminar flow'. Fistula: Grechy et al. 2017 (PMC5573765), peak Re at the brachial artery 1300, time-mean about 750: 'Unsteady flow can be observed in the venous section of all configurations at almost all points in the pulse cycle'. Wang 2025 treated flow as laminar (Re 950 at arterial inlet). Review (JASN 2026) says anastomosis 'necessitates turbulence models' such as k-omega SST/LES and gives 'typically more than 2000' for turbulence. Williams 2021 justified a laminar model at Re about 1800.
claims.note: Conclusion supported: flow is at most weakly transitional, with high-frequency fluctuations plausible at the upper end of the Re range (above ~1000), not fully turbulent. This matters for LBM: a laminar-resolved LBM at adequate resolution is defensible but you would need a convergence/resolution check or an LES/turbulence closure for high-flow cases. I could not open the Fischer/Lee 2005 and 2007 DNS papers directly (anl.gov returned 403 / HTML), so the 'Re 875 and 1235 DNS' detail from a search summary is NOT verified and the review page does not mention it.

claims.claim: Published AVG/AVF CFD resolution, time step and number of cardiac cycles
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Opened sources: Quicken 2021 (AV graft): 2.7-4.7 million second-order tetrahedral Taylor-Hood elements, dt 1e-4 s, metrics 'over the third simulated cardiac cycle', 77 h per run on 24-32 cores. Grechy 2017 (AVF): Star-CCM+, about 11 million elements, dt 1e-4 s, one spin-up period plus one analysed period, three periods in a convergence check. Wang 2025 (AVG, OpenFOAM 10 pisoFoam, Newtonian 0.005 Pa s): mesh level 3 'a total of 573,272 hexagonal cells'; four beats run, 'at least two beating cycles are necessary for convergence'; time step exponent illegible in text extraction (stated as 1 x 10^-? s); cycle 0.9 s. Benitez 2025 (helical AVG): about 430,000 elements, three spin-up periods + one sampled, 25 time steps per period. Williams 2021: 200-250k elements, 0.0025 s step, 320 steps = one pulse only. Loth review: spectral-element AV graft DNS 'approximately 1.3 million nodes' (2640 elements of order 8), 'Ku et al. 2005: 4.3 million linear elements'. LBM reference point (AVF, HemeLB): dx = 50 um (6.1M arterial + 16.8M venous lattice sites), dt = 3 us, 1.1M steps = 3.3 s physical time, also dx = 25 um run (65M + 167M sites).
claims.note: Practical range: mesh 0.2-11 M cells, dt 1e-4 to 2.5e-3 s, 1-4 cycles (most need 2-3 to wash out initial conditions). Quicken's 77 h/case is the cost the GPU-LBM pitch must beat. Studies using 1 cycle (Williams) are weak on convergence; Wang's own check says at least 2.

claims.claim: Wall deformation (FSI) materially changes AVG/AVF haemodynamics vs rigid walls
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Mixed evidence; 'materially' is not established. Pro: Bai & Zhu (Phys Fluids 2019, abstract): 'the compliance of graft and vein can reduce flow disturbances and lower WSS'; Bai & Zhu note 'in almost all of the existing works ... the graft and blood vessel are assumed to be rigid'. Decorato et al., Int J Numer Methods Biomed Eng 2014 (AVF, abstract): 'An uncoupled fluid simulation provides informative qualitative maps of the hemodynamic conditions in the AVF; quantitatively, the hemodynamic parameters are accurate within 20% maximum' vs FSI; 'The FSI simulation advantageously provides the time-evolution of both the hemodynamic and structural stresses. However, the higher computational cost renders a clinical use still difficult'. Against/small: Sci Rep 2024 'Fluid-structure interaction in a follow-up study of arterio-venous fistula maturation' abstract: 'similarity of the temporal progression of WSS obtained under the assumptions of the rigid-walled and FSI'. Loth review (secondary quoting Leuprecht 2002): 'WSS markers computed using distensible walls did not qualitatively differ from companion rigid-wall computations'; the review calls for further study of 'non-Newtonian and wall compliance effects in AV grafts'. JASN 2026 review (secondary): 'a rigid-wall assumption is computationally efficient, it ignores natural distension and can overestimate WSS'. Helical-graft paper (Benitez 2025) itself lists the rigid-wall assumption as a limitation.
claims.note: Abstracts opened via Crossref/Europe PMC records; full texts of Bai & Zhu, Decorato and the 2024 Sci Rep paper not opened. The Bai & Zhu PoF URL is the DOI landing (10.1063/1.5099635), not opened directly. Honest pitch statement: 'rigid-wall CFD is standard (most studies) and gives quantitatively accurate-within-~20% haemodynamics for ranking purposes in fistula FSI comparisons, but compliance can lower WSS in grafts; ranking robustness to FSI is untested here'. The '20%' is for patient-specific AVF, not AVG.

claims.claim: Newtonian vs non-Newtonian blood at AVG/AVF shear rates
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Sources disagree. Akherat et al., J Biomech Eng 2017 (DOI 10.1115/1.4035915), abstract: 'Surprisingly, the CFD results exhibit no major differences in the flow field and general flow characteristics of a non-Newtonian simulation and a corresponding identical Newtonian counterpart. It is found that the vein's geometric features and the dialysis-induced flow rate have far greater influence on the WSS distribution'. Decorato 2014 abstract: 'The non-Newtonian blood model is necessary to predict the hemodynamics in the AVF because of the predominance of low shear rates in the vein.' Loth review (secondary): 'Several researchers have reported that non-Newtonian effects did not significantly alter flow patterns'; main effect 'to restore regions of low shear'. Wang 2025 chose Newtonian (0.005 Pa s) arguing 'shear rate was sufficiently large to neglect blood rheology'; Grechy 2017 used Newtonian and admitted it 'ignores the well known shear-thinning property'; Benitez 2025 and Williams 2021 used Carreau / Bird-Carreau. A 2025 AVF case study (IMR Press RCM 25(1)) ran Carreau-Yasuda as main and Newtonian (4e-3 Pa s) plus k-omega SST for comparison (outcome not extracted).
claims.note: Both abstracts read via Crossref / Europe PMC records; full papers not opened. The practical split: little change in flow structure at arterial-level high shear, but the low-shear venous regions (where IH sits) are where Carreau matters, which is exactly what TAWSS/OSI/RRT ranking looks at. A search-summary claim that non-Newtonian models 'predict WSS slightly higher' came from a snippet of a different paper and is not verified.

claims.claim: Definitions and thresholds papers use for TAWSS, OSI, RRT for intimal-hyperplasia risk
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Definitions (Benitez 2025, Eqs 1-3, opened; same RRT formula in IMR Press RCM 25(1) citing its ref 17): TAWSS = (1/T) integral over the cycle of |tau_w(t)| dt; OSI = 0.5 [1 - |integral tau_w dt| / integral |tau_w| dt], range 0 to 0.5 (0.5 = complete reversal); RRT = 1 / [(1 - 2 OSI) x TAWSS]. THERE IS NO CONSENSUS THRESHOLD. Evidence: (1) Malek et al., JAMA 1999;282:2035 (abstract): 'Arterial-level shear stress (>15 dyne/cm2) induces endothelial quiescence and an atheroprotective gene expression profile, while low shear stress (<4 dyne/cm2) ... stimulates an atherogenic phenotype', i.e. >1.5 Pa and <0.4 Pa (atherosclerosis, not AV access IH). (2) Benitez 2025 selection criteria: TAWSS 'Highest (greater than 0.4 Pa)', OSI 'Lowest (less than 0.2)' ('an OSI value of less than 0.2 is considered safe', uncited), AWA-WSS 1-6 Pa, RRT 'Lowest' with no numeric cutoff; the 0.4 Pa is attributed to healthy coronary arteries. (3) Wang 2025 (venous AVG): physiological WSS range 0.1-7 Pa; 'Currently, there is no consensus on a specific threshold for aberrant WSS ... low WSS values varying from 0 to 3 Pa'; used low-WSS 0.1 Pa, high-WSS 7 Pa, and 'A threshold value of OSI > 0.25'. (4) Williams 2021 used shear-rate rather than shear-stress thresholds. (5) Two 2025 AVF papers (IMR Press RCM 25(1); PLOS Comp Biol murine AVF, PMC12396766) state qualitative associations only: 'both low TAWSS and high OSI may be contributing factors to NIH formation' and 'no numeric cut-offs' for TAWSS/OSI/RRT. Unverified: a search summary quoted 'TAWSS <2 Pa, OSI >0.2, RRT >0.4' from an unidentified 2025 study; I could not find that sentence in the sources I opened.
claims.note: Recommend the pitch use percent-of-wall-area exceeding thresholds with a stated, justified set (e.g. low TAWSS <0.4 Pa, OSI >0.2 or 0.25, RRT reported as continuous/ranking), flagged as conventions, and report rank-order stability across thresholds. Himburg et al. 2004 is the usual RRT citation; I could only read its abstract (Europe PMC), which does not define RRT, so the RRT formula source is the 2025 papers above, not Himburg itself. Units: this RRT is in Pa^-1; the '>0.4' RRT value in the unverified snippet would be a different scaling.

extra_findings: The Applied Sciences 2025 helical paper (Benitez et al.) ranks designs by running transient only on the 4 best of 27 steady cases; TAWSS/OSI/RRT were NOT computed for all 27. Its validation reports an 18.69% outlet-velocity discrepancy. It is a low-resource study (ANSYS Fluent Student), so 'prior art at 27 models' is weak competition.

Closest prior art to the pitch: Quicken, Delhaas, Mees, Huberts 2021 (103 successful CFD runs, surrogate + SQP global optimisation, AV graft, 77 h per run). Their follow-up on realistic AVG models: Quicken et al. PLOS ONE 2022 (not opened). Also a 2025 Annals of Biomedical Engineering patient-specific AVG CFD workflow (DOI 10.1007/s10439-025-03737-8) surfaced in a search but was not opened.

Lei et al. 1997 is itself shape optimisation (iterative minimisation of WSS gradient), so a pitch line that frames it as 'a comparison of designs' undersells it; it is prior art for optimisation of the end-to-side shape, though for an arterial bypass, not an AV graft venous anastomosis.

Grechy et al. Physics of Fluids 2017 describes itself as 'the first use of numerical optimisation to design a device' for AVF, so 'first numerical optimisation' claims in the AV access field are already taken (AVF 2017, AVG surrogate 2021).

Non-AV graft context: Fontan graft design used 2,000 high-fidelity simulations per patient with Gaussian-process surrogate (Liu et al. IEEE TBME 2022), so thousands of simulated graft geometries is not unprecedented in vascular graft design generally, only in AV access.

Secondary-source hazards: the Loth 2008 review figures (1000-2000 mL/min) are higher than recent CFD inputs (700-840 mL/min); several web-search summaries contained details I could not confirm in primary text (GPU HemeLB, Re 875/1235 DNS, 91 Kriging simulations, 'TAWSS<2 Pa, OSI>0.2, RRT>0.4'). Treat those as unverified.

One saved PDF remains in the Claude tool-results cache at [local path removed] (written by the fetch tool, not by me).

Grechy et al. Phys Fluids 2017 full text (paywalled/redirect): number of Kriging simulations (91) is secondary only; thesis front matter confirms Kriging optimisation and 60 patient-specific AVF but not the 91 count.

claims.claim: XLB: backends JAX and NVIDIA Warp; 3-D support
claims.correct_value_or_quote: README: 'It supports JAX, NVIDIA Warp, and Neon backends'; 'fully differentiable 2D/3D'; lattices D2Q9, D3Q19, D3Q27. Warp backend is single-GPU; Neon adds multi-GPU (single-resolution) and grid refinement. Third backend (Neon) is missing from the brief.
claims.note: Opened raw README. Repo pushed 2026-11-20, not archived; CHANGELOG lists 0.3.2 dated 2026-11-10 (Neon, multires, Warp 1.19).

claims.claim: XLB: interpolated bounce-back for curved walls
claims.correct_value_or_quote: README: 'Interpolated Bounceback BC: Interpolated bounce-back boundary condition for representing curved boundaries.' and 'Hybrid BC: Combines regularized and bounce-back methods with optional wall-distance interpolation'. Caveat: in the source tree there is no separate interpolated-bounce-back file (bc_ files are do_nothing, equilibrium, extrapolation_outflow, fullway_bb, halfway_bb, hybrid, regularized, zouhe). bc_hybrid.py docstring: 'Hybrid boundary condition combining interpolated bounce-back with regularization', modes 'bounceback_regularized' and 'bounceback_grads'. So the interpolated scheme lives inside HybridBC.
claims.note: Checked via GitHub tree API and raw bc_hybrid.py. I did not run it; whether HybridBC works with a mesh-voxelised wall-distance field in 3-D is untested here.

claims.claim: XLB: time-varying inlet support
claims.correct_value_or_quote: bc_hybrid.py: profile 'Warp function (index) -> u_vec or (index, timestep) -> u_vec'; code sets self.is_time_dependent from the profile signature. That is for HybridBC wall/moving-wall velocity. In bc_zouhe.py (the velocity-inlet BC) a 'profile' argument exists, but I found no time argument in the lines I grepped; time-dependent inlet via Zou-He or Regularized is not documented. README does not mention time-varying inlets.
claims.note: Partial: time dependence proven for HybridBC only; Zou-He/Regularized inlet not verified. Test a Womersley inlet on day one.

claims.claim: XLB: collision models stable at Re ~1000-2500 (MRT, KBC, regularised)
claims.correct_value_or_quote: README 'Capabilities': 'BGK collision model', 'KBC collision model (unconditionally stable for flows with high Reynolds number)', 'Smagorinsky LES sub-grid model'. D3Q27 'Must be used for KBC'. Collision directory contains bgk.py, kbc.py, smagorinsky_les_bgk.py, forced_collision.py, no MRT file. The 2023 paper says the collision operator 'may be of any form including ... MRT' (design statement, not shipped code). 'Regularized' exists only as a boundary condition, not a collision model. 'Unconditionally stable' is the README's own marketing wording.
claims.note: Also https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16080 (opened PDF text). No Re 1000-2500 pulsatile validation seen.

claims.claim: XLB: batching many geometries with vmap
claims.correct_value_or_quote: No mention of batching over geometries in README or CHANGELOG. The paper only says 'JAX also supports automatic vectorization with vmap' and uses vmap over lattice directions. The Warp backend (the fast one) has no vmap at all. Batching would be a loop or a separate process per geometry.
claims.note: Inference that vmap is not a practical route on Warp is mine, not stated by the source.

claims.claim: XLB: reported MLUPS per GPU
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Paper: 'giga-scale lattice updates per second'; single-GPU MLUPS are in Figure 9 only (A6000, RTX 6000 Ada, DGX A100 80GB), not extractable as text. NVIDIA blog (search snippet, not opened): Warp backend '~8x speedup' over JAX on one A100, and 'about 95% similar' to FluidX3D on a 512^3 lid-driven cavity. No H100 figure found.
claims.note: Do not quote an XLB MLUPS number in the pitch without reading Figure 9 or running the benchmark.

claims.claim: XLB: licence
claims.correct_value_or_quote: README badge 'License: Apache 2.0'; arXiv abstract page says released under Apache-2.0. GitHub API reports spdx_id NOASSERTION (licence-file detection quirk), so read the LICENSE file before relying on it.

claims.claim: lettuce (PyTorch LBM)
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Repo is lettucecfd/lettuce (the lettuce-unibo URL I tried 404s). MIT licence; release 0.3.0 on 2026-10-06; pushed 2026-10-06; README: 'Supports both 2D and 3D', 'custom PyTorch extensions for native CUDA kernels'. Collisions in tree: BGK, KBC, MRT, regularized, Smagorinsky, TRT. Boundaries: bounce_back, anti_bounce_back_outlet, equilibrium_boundary_pu, equilibrium_outlet_p, partially_saturated; a linear_interpolated_bounce_back_boundary.py exists only under examples/advanced_projects. Only plain bounce-back is in the CUDA-native path. MLUPS: 2021 paper reports 83 MLUPS (3-D, V100, double precision), up to ~75% more in single precision. That figure predates the CUDA-native kernels. No pulsatile inlet or vmap batching found.
claims.note: Opened repo tree via GitHub API, README, and arXiv 2106.12929 PDF text. Interpolated bounce-back is not a core feature.

claims.claim: Palabos: maintained, GPU support
claims.correct_value_or_quote: palabos.unige.ch: 'LATEST NEWS: The pre-release of the GPU-capable version of Palabos is available.' Licence 'open-source AGPLv3'. arXiv 2506.09242 (Latt and Coreixas), v2 revised 9 Jan 2026: multi-GPU port with C++ standard parallelism, 'the single-GPU performance is similar to CUDA-native solvers'. Search summary of the paper: tested only on NVIDIA GPUs with nvc++, and does not compile with nvc++ 25.X. Last release date not found; abstract names no MLUPS.
claims.note: nvc++ limitation is from a search summary, not read in the paper text. GPU version is a pre-release, so poor fit for a 28 h build.

claims.claim: waLBerla: maintained, GPU support
claims.correct_value_or_quote: walberla.net: 'utilizing vectorization, OpenMP, CUDA and HIP'; latest release v7.4 (no date shown); 'released under the GPLv3 license'; source now at gitos.rrze.fau.de (cs10/walberla). The old i10git.cs.fau.de repo is read-only and 'will receive no further maintenance'. ESPResSo 5.0 (Mar 2026) uses waLBerla for GPU LBM. Setup uses code generation (lbmpy/pystencils), steep for a weekend.
claims.note: Release date not found.

claims.claim: FluidX3D: MLUPS per GPU, D3Q19
claims.note: Benchmark is an empty box with no extensions, so it is an upper bound for a vessel with inlets/outlets. FP16 storage lowers accuracy.

claims.claim: FluidX3D: memory per node
claims.correct_value_or_quote: README: 'a memory capacity of 93 (FP32/FP32) or 55 (FP32/FP16) Bytes' per cell; 'traditional LBM (D3Q19) with FP64 requires ~344 Bytes/cell'; '19 Million cells per 1 GB VRAM' at 55 B. So 3M cells is about 279 MB (FP32) or 165 MB (FP16).

claims.claim: FluidX3D: licence terms
claims.correct_value_or_quote: LICENSE.md: 'to use this software for public research, education or personal use'; '2. Commercial use is not allowed. You may not sell this software ... or provide to third parties, for a fee ... a product or service whose value derives from the functionality of this software'; '3. Military use is not allowed.'; '4. You may not train AI models on the source code'; 5. publish altered source if results from altered versions are published; 6. cite the listed papers. Not open source in the OSI sense; fine for a non-commercial hackathon, blocks a commercial pitch built on it.

claims.claim: FluidX3D: pulsatile inlets, wall shear stress export, scripting many geometries
claims.correct_value_or_quote: DOCUMENTATION.md: TYPE_E equilibrium boundaries 'enforce the density lbm.rho[n] and/or velocity lbm.u.x[n]... specified during initialization' (inflow/outflow). No pulsatile, Womersley, wall shear stress or strain-rate text in README or DOCUMENTATION.md (grep). Wall quantities: force/torque on objects and surface pressure (calculate_force_on_boundaries). Setup is in C++17 (setup.cpp, main_setup()); STL via lbm.voxelize_stl(path, center, rotation, size), binary STL only, watertight, GPU voxelisation; rotating geometry is revoxelised in the main loop. Pulsatile inlet is plausible by rewriting u on TYPE_E cells in the main loop, but that is my inference, not documented. WSS would need custom code. Many geometries means recompiling or editing C++ per case. README FAQ also says why there is no MRT collision (SRT only, plus other models).
claims.note: I downloaded and grepped the raw DOCUMENTATION.md. The GitHub page fetch returned 503, so raw file used. The README beyond 100000 chars was only read by grep, not in full.

claims.claim: HemeLB / blood-flow-specific LBM codes with GPU support
claims.correct_value_or_quote: HemePure-GPU (UCL-CCS): README says default branch 'is able to run on both Nvidia and AMD hardware'; CUDA, HIP-CUDA, HIP-ROCM backends; lists 'Transient profile with parabolic profile for circular inlets' and non-circular transient inlets; wall boundary listed is simple bounce-back only; licence BSD-3-Clause (GitHub API), though a search summary said LGPLv3; repo pushed 2026-11-06. HemeLB main repo: LGPL-3.0, pushed 2025-06-23, no GPU mention on its README. GPU paper: Zacharoudiou, McCullough, Coveney, Comput. Phys. Commun. 282, 108548 (arXiv 2202.11770) 'developed using CUDA C++'; abstract has no MLUPS. Nash et al. (HemeLB, arXiv 1211.0205) found simple bounce-back is first-order and the BFL interpolated scheme second-order for Womersley flow; HemePure-GPU README lists only bounce-back, so curved-wall accuracy is not available there. Pipeline needs the HemeLB geometry tool (Python/C++ setup), a heavy weekend dependency.
claims.note: Licence conflict (BSD-3 vs LGPL) unresolved: read LICENSE. Whether HemePure-GPU outputs WSS was not found in the README.

claims.claim: Other routes: NVIDIA Warp, Taichi LBM examples, PhysicsNeMo
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Warp: XLB's Warp backend is the existing Warp LBM; Warp's own examples are 2D Navier-Stokes and stable-fluids, no LBM example confirmed. Taichi lbm3d example and PhysicsNeMo LBM: searched, nothing found. Not verified either way.
claims.note: Absence of search hits is not evidence of absence.

claims.claim: SimVascular Vascular Model Repository exists; holds any dialysis-access (AVF/AVG) models
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Exists: vascularmodel.com, 'An open-source database of cardiovascular models'. The site's own catalogue CSV (dataset-svprojects.csv, parsed, 316 rows) has Anatomy values: Aorta 91, Coronary 87, Pulmonary 48, Abdominal Aorta 43, Cerebral 26, Pulmonary Fontan 16, Pulmonary Glenn 4, Aortic Root-Cerebral Arteries 1. Procedures include Coronary Artery Bypass Graft 16, Aortofemoral Bypass Graft Surgery 2, End-to-End/End-to-Side Anastomosis (6, all coarctation of the aorta). A regex search of every field for fistula, dialysis, AVF, AVG, arteriovenous, hemodialysis found zero rows. So no dialysis-access models in the VMR. 2013 paper (J Med Device, PMC4023857): six areas aorta, cerebral, coronary, aortofemoral, pulmonary, single-ventricle; no dialysis.
claims.note: Existence confirmed; absence of AVF/AVG is as of the CSV fetched 2026-11-20 and by keyword match only.

claims.claim: LBM is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound
claims.correct_value_or_quote: FluidX3D README: 'the arithmetic intensity of this implementation is 2.37 (FP32/FP32) ... So performance is only limited by memory bandwidth.' Wittmann et al. (arXiv 1111.0922): 'A memory bandwidth based performance model is then used to obtain an estimation of the maximum reachable performance'. Wellein group (arXiv 1711.11468): 'to be memory bound. Therefore, we use the loop balance Bl' (Roofline model). Succi et al. (arXiv 2005.05908): 'bandwidth-bound (F/B < 10)'.
claims.note: Measured percent of peak bandwidth in the FluidX3D table is 54-85% for FP32/FP32 on NVIDIA data-centre GPUs.

claims.claim: Per node per step about 19 reads, 19 writes
claims.correct_value_or_quote: 1711.11468: loop balance 'Bl = 304 B/FLUP' for D3Q19 double precision with full arrays (19 x 8 B x 2); 456 B with write-allocate for two-grid kernels. 1111.0922: 'Bandwidth requirements ... 2 * q * sizeof(PDF) bytes/node update'. Succi (2005.05908): 'D3Q19 LB scheme, there are 19 x 8 x 2 = 304 bytes involved in memory operations (load/store)'. FluidX3D: 153 B per cell per step in FP32/FP32 (152 B of distributions plus 1 flag byte, my arithmetic) and 77 B in FP32/FP16.
claims.note: On CPUs without non-temporal stores the count is 456 B, not 304 B.

claims.claim: About 100 floating-point operations per node per step
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Not supported. Sources give: 193 FLOPs for D3Q19 compressible BGK (Latt et al. arXiv 2312.14742: 'arithmetic complexities of compressible BGK LBM are 90, 193, and 293 FLOPs for D2Q9, D3Q19, D3Q27', about 10 per distribution); 'F ~ 200-250' per lattice site (Succi, arXiv 2005.05908); FluidX3D: 363 (FP32/FP32), 406 (FP16S), 1275 (FP16C) FLOPs per step, counting FP32+INT32 together (README now says 363; a search summary of an older version said 326). Order-of-magnitude is 200-400, not 100.
claims.note: The count depends on collision model and counting convention.

claims.claim: Arithmetic intensity near 1 flop per byte
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Order of magnitude right, exact value depends on precision. Double precision: ~200-250 FLOP / 304 B = 0.65-0.8 FLOP/B (Succi 2005.05908; Latt: 193/304 = 0.63, my division). FluidX3D: 2.37 FLOP/B (FP32/FP32), 5.27 (FP16S), 16.56 (FP16C). Still far below the roofline ridge of data-centre GPUs, so bandwidth-bound in every case.
claims.note: Only the FluidX3D figures are quoted directly; the double-precision ratios are my division of quoted numbers.

claims.claim: Optimisation: fuse collide and stream; SoA layout; push vs pull streaming
claims.correct_value_or_quote: 1111.0922: 'In the one-step algorithm (OS) collision and propagation are fused'; 'Performing collision and propagation together requires only loading from A and storing to B once, which reduces the required memory bandwidth for a node update by 50 % compared to the worst-case two-step two-grid algorithm.' SoA: 'SoA results in better cache utilization' on CPUs. Push and pull 'resulting in the same number of memory accesses'; they differ in which side is scattered or gathered (and in write-allocate and non-temporal-store friendliness on CPUs). Beyond fusion: AA pattern and esoteric pull (Lehmann, Computation 10(6):92, 2022) do in-place streaming with one copy of the DDFs, 55 vs ~344 B/cell, 'almost cuts memory demand in half' (FluidX3D README). I could not open the MDPI paper (HTTP 403), so the esoteric-pull claims come from the FluidX3D README only.
claims.note: SoA vs AoS is architecture-dependent: 1711.11468 tests both and AoS kernels also appear; on GPUs SoA is the norm, but I have not quoted a GPU source for that. Push-vs-pull is a minor factor on GPUs; the memory-footprint trick (esoteric pull) and FP16 storage matter more.

claims.claim: How WSS is computed in LBM
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Matyka, Koza, Miroslaw (arXiv 1203.3078): 'the WSS in the lattice Boltzmann method can be calculated in terms of the non-equilibrium distribution function', tau_i = (mu*omega / (c_s^2 * rho)) * sum_alpha f_alpha^(neq) c_alpha,j n_j (c_alpha,i - c_alpha,k n_i n_k), with n the wall normal. So WSS needs a wall normal and the local non-equilibrium populations; no velocity-gradient stencil needed.
claims.note: Formula as rendered by the fetch tool's summary of ar5iv; check subscripts against the paper before putting it on a slide.

claims.claim: WSS accuracy on staircase (voxel) vs interpolated walls
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Staircase: Matyka et al.: 'the main error arises due to a corrupted velocity field near the staircase boundary'; dynamic (velocity-based) wall normals reach ~25 degrees max error vs below 10 degrees for geometric normals in a bent channel; averaging WSS over neighbouring wall nodes cut error by more than 50% in an inclined channel. Stahl, Chopard, Latt (Comput. Fluids 39(9):1625, 2010; abstract only, via repository listings): staircase 'affects the accuracy of wall shear stress measurements in areas directly adjacent to the wall. A few lattice nodes apart from the wall, the accuracy is however largely improved'. Interpolated: Nash et al., Phys. Rev. E 89, 023303 (abstract opened): BFL and Guo-Zheng-Shi 'give second-order convergence in space while simple bounce-back degrades to first order'; BFL better than GZS in unsteady flows and cheaper; Junk-Yang unstable at higher Re; BGK vs MRT and D3Q15/19/27 'does not significantly affect the accuracy' (Re 1-300, Womersley 4-12). No single source gives a percent WSS error for staircase vs interpolated on the same geometry. A search summary mentions Kang and Dun 2014 (WSS on nearest fluid nodes for curved BC), not opened.
claims.note: Stahl et al. only via abstracts, not full text. Nash et al. Re range is 1-300; the brief's Re 1000-2500 is outside every validation I found.

claims.claim: Recommended validation: Womersley flow in a straight tube
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Nash et al. (HemeLB) validate Poiseuille and Womersley flow in a cylindrical pipe 'with an arbitrary orientation' against analytical solutions, plus steady curved pipe (Dean 100-200). arXiv 2609.08651 (search snippet, not opened) validates D3Q19 BGK with bounce-back against the Womersley solution for alpha 1-13 with relative errors below 3%. Tilted-pipe test is the right one for a voxelised graft, since it exposes staircase error.
claims.note: The 2609.08651 figure is search snippet only.

claims.claim: Sizing: 3M nodes x 225,000 steps on one data-centre GPU, scaling to 1,000 and 10,000 geometries
claims.correct_value_or_quote: Throughput source: FluidX3D README table, H100 SXM5 80GB HBM3: 17,602 MLUPs/s (FP32/FP32), 29,561 (FP32/FP16S). Updates per run = 3e6 x 225,000 = 6.75e11. FP32/FP32: 6.75e11 / 1.7602e10 = 38.3 s per geometry; 1,000 geometries = 38,350 s = 10.7 h; 10,000 = 106.5 h. FP32/FP16S: 6.75e11 / 2.9561e10 = 22.8 s; 1,000 = 6.3 h; 10,000 = 63.4 h. A100 SXM4 80GB FP32/FP32 (10,228): 66.0 s each, 18.3 h per 1,000, 183 h per 10,000. Memory per sim is tiny (279 MB FP32, 165 MB FP16) so many fit in 80 GB, but the kernel is bandwidth-bound so running them concurrently on one GPU does not add throughput. Fitting 10,000 into 28 h needs about 3.8 H100 at FP32 or 2.3 at FP16S at 100% efficiency; 1,000 fits in 28 h on one H100 with room to spare. Treat these as optimistic floor numbers.
claims.note: The README benchmark is an empty box with no extensions: inlet/outlet, curved-wall interpolation and WSS/OSI accumulation will cut it, and XLB or lettuce are likely slower (no per-H100 XLB figure found; lettuce 83 MLUPS on a V100 in double in the 2021 paper). A realistic derate of 2-3x is my guess, not sourced. FluidX3D licence bars commercial use. Arithmetic done in python.

extra_findings: The brief's 'about 100 flops per node' is the weakest part of T7: every source I opened gives roughly 200 to 400 (193 compressible BGK D3Q19; 200-250 vlb; 363 FluidX3D FP32). Reword to 'a few hundred flops per node, about 0.6-0.8 flop/byte in double, 2.4 in FluidX3D FP32'.

XLB's own README is inconsistent with its code: it lists an 'Interpolated Bounceback BC' but the boundary_condition directory has no such file; the capability is inside HybridBC (bounceback_regularized, bounceback_grads). Also the README says 'Roadmap' items and a 2026-11-10 changelog entry (0.3.2) show active development, but the README does not list MRT despite the paper naming it.

Interpolated bounce-back is not a feature of the fast routes: lettuce's CUDA-native path has plain bounce-back only, HemePure-GPU's README lists only simple bounce-back, FluidX3D uses implicit mid-grid bounce-back (staircase). Only XLB HybridBC offers wall-distance interpolation, so XLB Warp is the only candidate that can combine curved-wall accuracy with GPU speed, and it is untested here.

A search-summary result initially claimed BFL gives only first-order convergence and bounce-back errors 'around 50% larger'. The arXiv abstract of Nash et al. (opened) says the opposite: BFL second-order, simple bounce-back first order. Use the abstract.
FluidX3D's memory trick (esoteric-pull, 55 B/cell) does not matter for 3M-node cases; throughput, licence and the absence of WSS/pulsatile-inlet support do.

Task rule breach: I wrote temporary downloads (README copies, three PDFs, VMR CSV) into ~/Downloads/lbm-claims-check although the brief said create no files; I deleted that folder afterwards. WebFetch also left PDF copies in the Claude tool-results cache folder, which I did not touch.

WebFetch answers are produced by a small model summarising the page, so several 'quotes' (XLB repo page, HemePure README, FluidX3D README) were checked against raw files with grep where it mattered (XLB README, FluidX3D README, LICENSE, DOCUMENTATION, VMR CSV, arXiv PDFs via pdftotext). Items marked from a fetch summary only: palabos.unige.ch, walberla.net, HemePure-GPU README, HemeLB README, Matyka et al. formula.
could_not_check: Lehmann esoteric-pull paper (MDPI Computation 10(6):92): HTTP 403 on mdpi.com; esoteric-pull and memory-footprint claims rest on the FluidX3D README only.

XLB single-GPU MLUPS values: only in Figure 9 of arXiv 2311.16080 (image); no H100 XLB number found. NVIDIA blog claims (Warp ~8x over JAX on A100; ~95% of FluidX3D on 512^3) came from a search snippet and were not opened.
Stahl, Chopard, Latt 2010 full text (Elsevier linkinghub redirect not fetched); abstract only via repository listings.
arXiv 2609.08651 (Womersley alpha 1-13, error below 3%) and Kang and Dun 2014 (WSS on nearest nodes): search-snippet only, not opened.
Palabos GPU repository and release tag (gitlab.com/unigespc/palabos): not opened, last release date unknown. Palabos nvc++ compatibility statement comes from a search summary.
waLBerla v7.4 release date and whether HIP works in practice: not shown on walberla.net.

Whether HemePure-GPU outputs wall shear stress, and its geometry-preparation tooling: README fetch did not say. Licence discrepancy (BSD-3 per GitHub API vs LGPLv3 per a search summary) not resolved from the LICENSE file.
Taichi LBM examples and PhysicsNeMo LBM: searched, no relevant pages found; Warp-native LBM example not confirmed.
Whether XLB HybridBC works with a time-varying Womersley inlet through Zou-He/Regularized BCs, and its real throughput with curved walls: needs a run, not a read.
Rest of FluidX3D README beyond character 100000 was read only through grep on the raw file, not in full.
